doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

title: Studying with Sanford Gold, paid for by Ruby Braff
summary: Ruby Braff urges lessons with Sanford Gold; Braff and Bradley offer to pay, and Gold's gift for hearing fingerings.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: About 15 or so. Yeah. And one last thing that was probably a real key component of all these things in terms of getting into school and becoming more professional was that at the Jazz Museum one of Jack Bradley’s closest friends was the cornetist Ruby Braff. And Ruby was a real character and I eventually became his personal manager and that’s another story. But Ruby heard me play the piano at the museum, as much as I could play, and he kind of said you know it’s pretty bad he says, but you know you’ve got some potential there. You really should study with this guy named Sanford Gold, who was kind of a legendary — well I didn’t know — kind of a legendary piano teacher in New York in the 60s, 70s, maybe 50s, 60s, 70s, and all kinds of people studied with him from A to Z classical, jazz, he taught technique but he also married the study of the piano into theory. So as you learned — I mean he didn’t teach beginning players but as you learned to play this Chopin etude or as you learned to play “Waltz for Debby” or whatever it was, you were mapping out the harmonic sphere. And he had his own system of diminished chords and substitution chords and all this kind of stuff. It was pretty good. And so I studied with — so what happened was he charged $25 a lesson. This was 1973 or so. And that was unheard of. I mean I was taking piano lessons in Ridgewood, New Jersey for, I don’t know, for $5 or $10. And my parents were really skeptical. And one day when my dad came to pick me up at the Jazz Museum Ruby came out with Jack Bradley and they talked to my father. My dad didn’t know who Ruby Braff was except that Jack probably said he’s a great musician. He said, “Mr. Schoenberg, you know, your son has some talent but he’s really not too good but if he has any potential he should go with Sanford Gold, it’s $25.” And he said, “I’m sorry but we can’t, we’re not going to do that.” And Ruby and Jack said, “Well we’ll pay for it then.” Now whether they really would have or not I don’t know, it doesn’t make a difference. But the gesture of having said that convinced my parents that I should study with Sanford Gold and that is probably the most significant thing that happened to me in between playing the piano at four years old and getting into Manhattan School of Music as a piano minor, third year piano minor when I was 17 or 18. Because Sanford Gold could hear wrong fingering. He could hear wrong fingering. And it’s not just me saying it, he was famous for it. He’d be in another part of the room facing another way while you were playing, and he’d say, “Second finger.” I mean he could tell from the articulation of the note. Now also studying with him at that time were Jon Faddis and Lew Soloff, who were both new in New York and roommates I guess, or very close friends, and they were studying with him. They couldn’t have been, I mean Jon is not that much older than me, he was probably 19 or something. And I remember they were crazy and I remember meeting other people in those days at his © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
studio. So if you put all that together it starts to give you a picture of where I was when I went to college.
